CORRECTION OF COMMENTS DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday in the House of Commons during Question Period, on the basis of information that had been given to me, I made reference to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) having commented in the past on an RCMP inquiry into Mr. Sinclair Stevens.
Later, in Question Period, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) pointed out that there had been no such RCMP inquiry into Mr. Stevens' activities. The Minister of Finance is, of course, quite right. There was of course only the Parker Commission.
I accept the correction and would want the record corrected immediately because I would not want to mislead the House.

subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations) moved
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-10, an Act relating to the forgiveness of debts incurred or assumed in respect of
certain official development assistance loans made by the Government of Canada to the governments of certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly today to the Bill tabled in the House for the purpose of forgiving the debts incurred or assumed in respect of official development assistance by a number of sub-Saharan countries in Africa.
My comments will mainly concern the three following points: First, the decision to have this Bill approved by Parliament is in line with Canada's policy on Third World debt problems; second, the Bill will make it possible for Canada to honour the commitments it made sometime ago; and finally, this measure has practically no impact on our country's Budget.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all parliamentarians are aware of the serious problems confronting debtor countries in the Third World.
I will not provide an in-depth analysis of the causes although I will name a few: the oil crises of the past fifteen years, sagging market prices for raw materials, problems encountered in obtaining access to the markets of industrialized countries, soaring interest rates, and so forth.
It is important to understand that these are factors over which debtor countries have very little control. However, the debts are a tremendous burden for the African countries concerned, which are already faced with formidable obstacles, including vulnerable ecosystems, increasing desertification and a precarious food production system.
In absolute terms, the debts of sub-Saharan countries are not as onerous as those of Latin American countries.
However, considering the level of economic development and scarce resources of the countries concerned, the impact is far more devastating.

May 26, 1989
Sub-Saharan Africa
Canada has already taken many initiatives in favour of debt distressed countries. The steps now being proposed are therefore part of a process that our country set in motion during the previous decade.
In 1977 we forgave the Official Development Assistance debts of 12 countries on the list of the least developed countries. Since April, 1986 we have been providing all new bilateral development assistance to all countries in the form of grants only, rather than loans that would add to the debt burden of Third World countries.
In 1986 Canada announced a moratorium on Official Development Assistance debt repayment for African countries that are implementing a structural adjustment program.
In 1987 Parliament also forgave the ODA debts of Togo, Mauritania, and the now defunct East Africa Community. The international community, especially African countries, welcomed those initiatives. They viewed them as proof of our country's commitment to help distressed countries.
At the 1987 Venice Summit, Canada announced that it would provide help to the poorest countries, and at the Toronto Summit last year Canada continued to play a leadership role concerning solutions to the debt problem.
Within the relevant international fora we are encouraging a flexible approach, including the possibility of rescheduling repayments and utilizing concessional interest rates on short-term loans to low income countries.

Mr. Speaker, in March 1988 I tabled our Official Development Assistance Strategy, entitled: Sharing our Future. For the first time, this document includes an Official Development Assistance Charter, in which Canada has made helping the world's poorest countries a priority.
Clearly, the Bill before the House today is entirely in line with that objective.
Furthermore, Canada has decided to facilitate the implementation of structural adjustment programs in debtor countries. The programs will help these countries to improve their economic and financial situation, while
remaining sensitive to the needs of the most vulnerable groups.
The proposed legislation also follows through on commitments we made before two international forums. You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that in September 1987, at the Sommet de la Francophonie held in Quebec, Canada announced its intention to forgive the debts of a certain number of sub-Saharan member countries.
We announced a similar measure for the benefit of African members of the Commonwealth, at a meeting of Commonwealth heads of State which we hosted shortly afterwards in Vancouver.
However to respond to the pressing needs of these countries, Canada must honour its commitments without delay.
The countries targeted by the proposed legislation are: Cameroon, the Ivory Coast, the Congo, Gabon, Ghana, Kenya, Madagascar, Nigeria, Senegal, Swaziland, Zaire, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Since we must assume that when preparing their budgets, these countries allowed for the consequences of the measures announced by Canada, they would find it very hard to understand, and with them the rest of the international community, any failure on our part to honour these commitments.

I now turn to the third point to which I referred earlier, namely that the proposed legislation has virtually no tangible impact on Canada's budgetary situation. This is without question an important element in the current context. One has to understand that our country's Official Development Assistance loans are highly concessional in nature. As a practical matter, the grant element makes up over 90 per cent of those loans. They are considered budgetary items, which means that Parliament has already appropriated the necessary resources for the loans through budgetary estimates. Therefore, the removal of those loans will not entail any new appropriations, nor will it impact on the cumulative deficit.
I would like to add-and this is another important point-that if the sums in question were repaid, Canada's Official Development Assistance disbursements would be increased by corresponding amounts. This occurs because Canada's Official Development Assistance, as a proportion of our Gross National Product, is
May 26, 1989

based on net disbursements, that is, disbursements less Official Development Assistance loan repayments.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize again that this Bill continues a policy Canada has long followed. We are convinced that the African countries concerned cannot return to the path of true development unless their debt burden is lightened. A consensus was reached on this subject very recently at a joint meeting of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.
To be sure, the debts owed to Canada are only a part of the total indebtedness of Third World countries. Nevertheless, we are convinced that in honouring its commitments, our country will encourage other creditor countries to do their share. That is what has just happened at the Francophone Summit in Dakar, when French President Francois Mitterrand announced that his country would cancel the official development assistance debts incurred by several poor African countries. We are pleased with this decision, which is similar to the initiatives that Canada announced in 1987 at the Francophone Summit in Quebec City and the Commonwealth meeting in Vancouver.
We note with satisfaction that the trend to concrete action in this crucial area is growing. We again express the wish that other countries will take similar action. For its part, Canada continues to consider other ways to act and contribute to the solution of this pressing problem.

subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for the opportunity for responding to the proposed Bill C-10, which will forgive debt in 13 sub-Saharan African countries.
I would like to say at the outset that it is indeed difficult to vote against such a Bill. If anybody has been watching, for example. The Journal program which is focusing on the plight of people in the Sudan and will continue this evening, one will recognize the dire need of so many hundreds of thousands of people in Africa; not just Africa but throughout the developing world, the Third World.
Sub-Saharan Africa
In the past years Canadians have responded very openly and generously to the plight of people in the Third World. When polls are taken, they indicate that over 70 per cent of Canadians support the generous past experience and policies of the Canadian Government in the provision of overseas Official Development Assistance to developing nations. They are scandalized by the recent cut-backs of this Government in its official overseas development assistance.
I have two problems with this Bill which I would like to address today. The first one is that I would not, standing here proposing to support Bill C-10, want to suggest that I am in any way supporting this Government in trying to recuperate its tarnished image in relationship to its non-support of Third World countries. In fact. Bill C-10 amounts to a big zero. It says nothing new. The Bill was first suggested in May, 1986 when we put a moratorium on debt in African countries. Since that time, and as per our policy from 1977 that any loans or payments made to Third World countries would only be accepted by them as grants, those countries have not had to make any payments to this country. Therefore, this Bill purporting now to forgive loans is a zero. Mr. Speaker, if you subtract zero from zero you will always have zero, and that is what this Bill represents.
The Government has been extremely irresponsible in dealing with Third World debt problems. Third World debt is one of most serious problems that the world faces today, yet the Government has no policy. It abrogates all its responsibility for dealing with the problem to the international financial institutions. That is not good enough.
The substance of Bill C-10 is meaningless. Little has been said so far about the Government's cuts to Overseas Development Assistance, but more will be said because 70 per cent of Canadians will not forget what the Minister has permitted to occur in Third World countries in terms of our caring and concern and the outward signs of that to Third World countries.
As the Minister has stated, the Bill has no impact on the budget of our country. This Bill is definitely not representing in any way any new generosity on the part of the Government. In the Government's own documents with regard to this issue it states: "The financial costs of the legislation are virtually nil. As a result of the concessional nature of ODA loans, ODA loans are considered budgetary, meaning that Parliament has ap-

May 26, 1989
Sub-Saharan Africa
propriated the necessary resources for the loans through budgetary Estimates. Removal of these loans from the accounts of Canada will therefore not entail any new appropriations nor will it impact on the cumulative deficit."
In this Bill the amount that is suggested to be forgiven is approximately $672 million. Had that been repaid, it would automatically have been added to CIDA's budget to ensure that Canada's net ODA levels did not diminish due to debt repayment. However, I reiterate that zero from zero is always zero.
In looking at the Bill and the forgiveness of debt of $672 million, it is interesting to compare that figure with the total debt in only three of the thirteen African countries listed in this Bill.
As of 1986, the debt in Nigeria alone was $16.6 billion; the debt in the Ivory Coast was $7.4 billion; and the debt in Zaire was $4.6 billion. Therefore, the supposed forgiveness of $672 million has very little significance. It is the greater debt that is the true burden of those countries,concerning which the Government refuses to confront and develop policies.
With regard to the Government and its lack of commitment to the Third World countries and also dealing with debt, it is interesting to look at the actual record of the Government with this Budget. Normally, Official Development Assistance amounts to approximately 3 per cent of Government expenditures. With this Budget, Official Development Assistance has absorbed 29 per cent of all the expenditure cuts made by the Government. Where are the cuts?
If we propose to show that we have a concern for African countries, it is interesting to look at the cuts in the Budget. For example, and I remind Members to think of the starving in Africa, bilateral and multilateral food aid cuts amount to $65 million this year. Where is the conscience of the Government?
International humanitarian assistance has been cut by $25 million. International NGOs, non-governmental organizations, those that reach out to the most in need in their own countries, have had their budget cut by $3 million. Voluntary sector support has been cut by $87 million. The budgets of Anglophone Africa and Francophone Africa have been cut by $33 million. This Bill represents zero.
What the Government has done through its Budget cuts to Official Development Assistance has indirectly and directly caused a diminishing of potential aid assistance to Africa of $203 million. The total cuts to Official Development Assistance this year amount to $360 million. That is $360 million less than last year's expenditures in ODA.
We expected that ODA would go up to $3.1 billion this year, if we had maintained our level of increasing ratios. Instead, Official Development Assistance expenditures will sit at $2.44 billion or .43per cent of our Gross National Product.
Years ago, when Mr. Pearson was Prime Minister, he set the benchmark for the ratio of ODA to GNP for the developing nations. He suggested that .7 per cent ratio ODA to GNP was the target that we should all be attempting to achieve. As a result of the Budget, we are experiencing the third drawback from that target put in place by this Government. As a matter of fact, the Government no longer even talks about .7 per cent ratio as an objective we are trying to achieve. By our calculations, we might be able to achieve such a target by the year 2040. However, in committee, members of the Government have suggested that it is unrealistic for us to even think of attempting to achieve .7 per cent ODA to GNP ratio. I believe that that is simply unconscionable. It is being heard by Canadians, and they will not forget.
Canada now ranks last among middle income developed countries as to its level of ODA provided. We are last when compared to other countries such as the four Nordic countries and Belgium, France and the Netherlands. Canada now joins the United States as being the only developed country that is cutting back its ODA-GNP ratio. Perhaps that is our country's new benchmark and model for developed nations.
The debt problem exists not only for sub-Saharan African countries. It exists world-wide. The world-wide debt now stands at more than $1 trillion U.S. In the developing nations of the world we have felt that we have been assisting Third World countries, helping them to become equal, and that we were providing them with economic and social justice. We have striven for those objectives over the years.
May 26, 1989

However, at the moment we are failing because when one looks at world-wide cash flows, the direction of net cash flow is not from the developed nations to the developing nations but it is quite the reverse. Annually, the developing nations are contributing $30 billion to the developed nations of the world. As the Minister says: "debtor countries have no control over interest rates" which are the factor that contributes very much to the realignment of net cash flows in the world. The Third World countries are defenceless against increasing rises in interest rates. Developed countries have some control over interest rates.
I repeat that the federal Government is taking no responsibility for addressing these problems as they affect Third World countries.
In the 1980s, developing countries have experienced a 30 per cent decline in their real per capita incomes. This decline is equivalent to what Canadians and other developed nations might have experienced during the dirty thirties of the depression. However, when we were going through that most difficult period, we did not have those additional problems of droughts, food shortages and rising debt. We did not experience at the same rate the institutional deterioration that the Third World is experiencing now.
This year, 40,000 children are dying in this world every day from malnutrition and disease. Canada has abrogated its responsibility to deal with international debt problems. It has abrogated this responsibility to international financial institutions which receive in the order of 18 per cent of our ODA.
International financial institutions have instituted programs like structural adjustment programs, or SAPS, economic recovery programs, or ERPS. SAPS and ERPS all give us indigestion and they are doing nothing to assist Third World countries. They are most inappropriate. These programs have produced nothing but deterioration of the standard of living and have added to the inequality and injustices that exist in Third World countries.
Let us look at some of the background of Bill C-10. It was my honour and privilege in June, 1986, to be present at the United Nations Special Session which addressed the economic crisis in Africa. I was present as a member
Sub-Saharan Africa
of the non-governmental organization community in Canada. The purpose of our community being at the United Nations was to afford non-government organizations from Africa the opportunity to be present and to be heard in that forum which was discussing the crisis in their countries.
We realize that the people of Africa have very little say in what their governments do and the decisions and policies that are taken by their governments. Therefore, it was our concern as Canadians, as non-governmental organizations of a developed country, to afford these non-governmental organizations of Africa the opportunity to be heard and to speak.
It was with pride at that time that I heard our former Minister of External Relations stand up and make her statement to the program of Africa 2,000 in which she set a moratorium on debt repayments. I cannot help but believe she must have taken some of her directions in making this statement from our ambassador to the United Nations at that time.
There was a dialogue and a debate going on at the United Nations at the time, whereby leaders of large developed countries such as Britain, the United States and Germany, were suggesting that the issues of debt and financial matters, when discussing an economic crisis in Africa, had to be left within the realm of the international financial institutions and could not be discussed at the United Nations. Our Government, by presenting its statement, boldly said that yes, indeed, debt was an appropriate topic of discussion at the United Nations.
The Minister made the following statement:
Today I am announcing that Canada is offering to sub-Saharan countries a moratorium on repayment of these loans for an initial period of five years. We are prepared to extend this measure in five-year segments until the year 2000. In this way, we wish to help in providing all the countries of sub-Saharan Africa that face serious external payments difficulties and that have demonstrated a commitment to undertake necessary economic adjustment, the room to manoeuvre that they need to put their economies back on a solid foundation.
On a country-by-country basis, we are prepared to immediately begin discussing the application of this measure within the framework of World Bank Consultative Groups or in other appropriate forums.
I draw to the attention of the House the Minister's reference to putting a moratorium on repayments to

May 26, 1989
Sub-Saharan Africa
African countries that have demonstrated a commitment to undertake necessary economic adjustment.
It changes. At the Venice summit in June, 1987, comments were made again about this moratorium. The Government proposed a paper to be discussed, which dealt with debt relief. It said:
The most dramatic and helpful action would be to convert all existing ODA loans to grants-Another option would be to extend the moratorium on repayments for a given number of years or until a country achieves a certain level of development as measured by the objectives indicators outlined later in this paper-such relief would be extended to countries meeting agreed criteria and undertaking serious adjustment efforts under the IMF or World Bank.
This statement was further elaborated upon on June 30 by the present Minister when she referred to Bill C-62. She said:
The non-repayment period could also be extended by another five years if the economy of these countries showed no signs of recovery.
This is certainly a different tone from that in which the moratorium and forgiveness was originally suggested. Countries that have demonstrated a commitment to undertake necessary economic adjustment is quite different from a statement that says that the Government would provide debt relief to countries that showed no sign of recovery.
It is very important that countries that are experiencing debt and that do experience moratoriums or forgiveness of debt do exhibit some concern for changing their own internal policies. When it was originally stated that our moratorium was based on that fact, we supported it.
There are many countries in Africa that do not stand for equality and justice in their own countries. Anyone visiting those countries would have a difficult time experiencing social justice after seeing the presidents of these countries drive down crowded city streets at 90 miles an hour in stretch limousine Mercedes. Unfortunately many of these countries, not just in their economic and justice policies, but on human rights, exhibit a lack of caring for the people.
When Canada makes concessions, it should be more thoughtful and responsible. I have attempted to discover exactly what commitments Canada was imposing on the sub-Saharan African countries, on a country by country
basis, to see whose debt is being forgiven in Bill C-10.1 could find nothing. There do not appear to have been any conditions attached, despite the Minister's original statement.
I have done research and I have asked the Library of Parliament to help me in this. I have found nothing. However, I refer to a Senate report of 1987 entitled: "Canada, the International Financial Institutions and the Debt Problem of Developing Countries". This a quote from that document:
The Canadian government has taken steps to lighten the official debt load of a number of low-income countries. During the Conference on International Economic and Co-operation in 1977 Canada forgave its outstanding loans to the least-developed countries, including eight African countries, for a total forgiveness of $310 million of debt. Since that time all CIDA projects in these least-developed countries in sub-Saharan Africa have been on a grant basis. Further, in 1986 Canada offered a 15-year moratorium on payments of principal and interest of the ODA debt of other low-income sub-Saharan African nations where Canada had continued to make concessional loans rather than grants. Debt of this nature totalled $700 million and involved forgoing $250 million in repayments.
Initially the Government offered a five-year moratorium, but announced that it was prepared to extend the measure in five-year segments until the year 2000. The Government asked only that the African countries affected show their commitment to introducing economic reforms.
None of them, it appears, have voluntarily offered to do this. The international financial institutions have imposed structural adjustment programs on them, which have been a total failure to these countries. The Government has taken no responsibility in trying to support actions on the part of sub-Saharan African countries to introduce their own reforms to bring about greater justice and equality within their own countries.
When the African nations came to the United Nations in June of 1986, they had met prior to that meeting to put together a statement which is called: "Africa's Priority Programme for Economic Recoveiy". It outlines what they wanted to do to bring about adjustment in their own countries. At the United Nations in June of 1986, the developed nations of the world were impressed. We were supportive of these statements that came out of African countries. They state in the priority statement: "The successful implementation of the Priority Programme will lay the foundation for durable structural changes.
May 26. 1989

improve levels of productivity and ensure the rapid recovery of the African economies".
It suggested immediate measures that could be taken to combat food emergencies, such as creating and sustaining national emergency preparedness, effecting early warning systems, establishing flexible and efficient regional networks of crop protection, and establishing national food security arrangements. Their program suggested medium-term measures, raising the level of investment in agriculture, increasing food production, establishing and protecting arable land and rendering it more productive.
These nations wanted to address their own programs and problems as they saw them. They wanted to devote time and resources to human resource development. They wanted to change radically the educational system at all levels to ensure that the skills, knowledge and attitudes that are relevant to Africa's developmental needs were generated. They wanted to intensify efforts to promote mass literacy and adult learning programs. They wanted to utilize efficiently manpower resources, including measures to reverse the brain drain, et cetera. They wanted to have the people of their country participate in development. In their own program they had put an emphasis on involving women in development.
All of these programs that they wanted to institute, however, required the assistance of the developed world. The international community responded by stating:
The international community is aware that ihe process of development being initiated by the African countries, as reflected in the Priority Programme, has to be supplemented by complementary actions of the international community through intensified cooperation and substantially increased support -
The international community recognizes the magnitude of Africa's debt and the severe and restrictive burden which this has placed on many African countries. It realizes that measures have to be taken to alleviate this burden and to enable those countries to concentrate on the full implementation of priorities. In addressing problems arising from such debt, existing mechanisms should respond flexibly and be improved as appropriate.
The Government has decreased in its Budget the level of overseas Official Development Assistance to sub-Saharan African countries. It has not responded as it
Sub-Saharan Africa
originally committed itself to respond on a country-bycountry basis, helping the African countries to meet their own objectives. It has not responded to the debt problems in those countries.
The Senate of Canada in 1987 addressed the problem of debt. The Government has not responded and taken action as a result of their report. It is worthwhile to mention some of the remarks that were made in it. As I stated before, the Senate report of 1987 is entitled: "Canada, the International Financial Institutions and the Debt Problem of Developing Countries". The Senate report suggests that there must be a dialogue between creditor and debtor countries. The report states:
The Committee considers that the time may have come for creditor governments to lift their objections to direct dialogue with debtor governments.
The Committee recommends that the Canadian government publicly endorse and advocate the principle of a dialogue within the IMF's Interim Committee involving creditor and debtor Governments.
- the Committee recommends the creation of a small group of distinguished persons from North and South which might be known as the Advisoty Group on International Indebtedness -
The tasks of this Advisory Group would be: to monitor the evolution of debt problems; to relate them to other aspects of the world economy; to comment on the performance of the IMF and the World Bank and their shortcomings; to strengthen the commitment of debtor countries governments to better management and adjustment; to increase the awareness of the problems of debt particularly of the poorest countries; and to help focus the attention of creditor countries on remedial measures.
A great deal of the basic work on how this country could profitably address the debt problems internationally and world-wide are suggested in this Senate report.
Other groups in the world have looked at the problem and have come up with their own recommendations. I would like to quote from a group called CIDSE which represents 14 Catholic development organizations located in Europe and North America. They suggest:
A debtor country is considered credit worthy if it accepts the IMF's "Recommendations for Adjustment" in a Letter of Intent.
Typical IMF adjustment measures include: limitation of the national budget deficit through measures to curb the growth of public spending such as the reduction of subsidies, price increases for public services,

May 26. 1989
Sub-Saharan Africa
staff cuts, restriction of the money supply and de-regulation of interest rates; limitation of wage increases;
Experience has shown that adjustment policies based on IMF's criteria had only limited success, whilst their social costs have been very high.
I would like to spend a few moments addressing the irresponsible abrogation of this Government's responsibility to deal with debt problems to the IMF and other international financial institutions. What we do need is structural adjustment with a human face. Elowever, structural adjustment the way it is affecting Third World countries now is having very deleterious effects on the populations of these countries.
Health costs in developing nations have had to be reduced 50 per cent world-wide. Education expenditures in developing nations world-wide have had to be reduced 25 per cent. I mentioned before that the net cash flows from developing nations to developed nations now amount to $30 billion per annum. Instead of the developed nations helping the Third World countries, the Third World countries are now helping us with cash flows to us. We are all backwards and upside down. The world needs to take a new look at structural adjustment.
Environmental degradation is carrying on at a heavy pace. The population is rising. If people do not know that their children are going to live, the population will rise. When people know they have security, that they can feed their children, and that their children will live in health and prosperity and survive, population rates immediately decrease. The Third World is experiencing tremendous food scarcity. There is deprivation of food causing tremendous costs to the future of the world in the disabilities that are resulting.
The present results of the relationship between the developed and the developing nations has caused incredibly huge rises in food shortages, housing shortages, water degradation, health care degradation and education degradation. Illiteracy is increasing. The opportunities in these countries to the poor of their countries are decreasing rapidly. We have had structural adjustment but we have had no revitalization and growth. Adjustment must be reconsidered. Debt world-wide must be rationally and humanely confronted.
This Government introduces bills to forgive debt but takes no leadership in dealing with the root causes of poverty and death. Debt forgiveness will not prevent new, unmanageable debt from mounting. As the world's poor become poorer, injustices become more evident. Frustration inevitably mounts. Poverty causes tension and violence and mounting poverty and inequality become a security issue. Desperation to have access to our world's natural resources will have irreversible environmental impacts. We will all lose.
I would like to conclude by saying that Bill C-10 is meaningless posturing. It highlights this Government's irresponsible attitude to a major world problem. I support this Bill but I implore the Government to address debt problems world-wide and fill a debt policy vacuum.

subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I am pleased to rise in support of Bill C-10, although I think it is somewhat ironic that we are forgiving a debt that we have already acknowledged could never be repaid. It is the old saw, that you cannot get blood from a stone.
In beginning my comments, because I only have a short time, I would just like to outline the direction I want to take on my response to this Bill.
First, I want to talk about the history of how sub-Saharan Africa incurred such a debt, how it got into the place it is in now and our complicity in getting it there. I then want to talk about the complexity that the subject demands, the definitions of terms such as structural adjustment and IFI, the International Financial Institutions, the IMF. For most Canadians, these terms are so obscure that I think they require definition. I also believe that our complicity in those financial institutions should be explained.
Then I would like to go to Canada's role in the forgiveness of debt. While the Government and Canadians generally should be applauded for the forgiveness of debt, we should be able to see this not in isolation. We have to see it in the context of the recent cut-backs to foreign aid, Official Development Assistance. To forgive the debt and then not to increase foreign aid is a contradiction.
To begin, then, I will just focus on the history. I have personal knowledge of the effects of the debt problem in Africa. I have travelled to the Sudan and to Eritrea. One of the most graphic pictures of the polarization that occurs in a country under IMF supervision as to its internal policies came to me when I walked out of my hotel in Khartoum. There in the street was a crippled beggar child-we do not know whether he was delib-
May 26, 1989

erately crippled-begging. He was beside a very scrawny donkey, and next to that donkey was a huge white Mercedes Benz limousine. That is what we see when the IMF runs things in Africa. There is no understanding of what IMF policies do. There is no understanding of the humanity that is harmed by their policies.
Julius Nyere, the former President of Tanzania, said that there is a way of focusing on the real reasons why this debt has happened. The Third World is blamed for its own poverty. The Third World heavy debt burden arose through a combination of modest development ambitions and external events beyond the control of developing countries.
What happened after the first oil shock of 1973 is that many Third World countries borrowed to ease their adjustment to the new fuel prices. Credit was easy to obtain as western banks looked for profitable uses of the OPEC surpluses which were being entrusted to them. I know that kind of dynamic as well, because prior to working for a non-governmental organization I was a banker. I know how banks work. When banks have surplus cash, they want to put it out there to make money from it. That is what happened. The Third World bought into it.
Nyere said: "The resulting huge debts are a national problem, not only for the debtor countries". He said: "We undertook to repay and honour the demands that we do so, but we are increasingly unable to do so because of the changes in world conditions since the debts were incurred. The debts are therefore also a problem for the developed countries".
That is the focus of what my main argument on this Bill is going to be.
We are in this together. We cannot see a forgiveness of sub-Saharan African debt in isolation from what is occurring in our own country. It is that connection with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank that we have to be cognizant of. In this interdependent world, if we do not understand those connections, we can go down the same road as they are going down.
In the moments that are allowed me before Question Period, I just want to draw the attention of the House to that interconnectiveness. Our own Budget deficit and the Government's approach to attacking the Budget deficit has parallels in the Third World. One agency, OXFAM Canada, likened our own Budget to a self-imposed IMF structural adjustment. On that note, I will draw my comments to a close and hope that at some future time I will be able to continue.

subsubtopic: STATE OF NORTHERN COD STOCK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the Harris task force released today indicates, and I quote from page 21:
The state of the stock does not support a conclusion that anything drastic or threatening has occurred to the northern cod stock to date.
However, measures will have to be put in place including, it would seem, a reduction in next year's TAC to ensure that the stock again begins to grow.
Over the next few months I expect we will see various suggestions put forth as to measures that should be put in place to deal with the problem. One measure already suggested by some that would be absolutely, unequivocally, completely unacceptable to all Nova Scotians would be any diminution whatever in the percentage of the historic participation, a participation that dates back well over two centuries, of Nova Scotian fishing vessels and Nova Scotia fishermen in this vitally important fishery, which Nova Scotians helped develop and from which the Nova Scotian economy and Nova Scotian fish plants and fish plant workers benefit so much.

May 26. 1989

subtopic: UNREST IN LEBANON-CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN CEASEFIRE
UNREST IN LEBANON-CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN CEASEFIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after 15 years of strife, Lebanon has become a scarred pained victim of aggression and destruction. This country has lost more than its status as the pearl of the Middle East. It has lost many of its precious young and its men and women. The strife is creating great stress on Lebanese Canadians and their families as a result of the devastating attacks and bombings to which Lebanon and its people have been subjected.

Canadians believe their country has always shown an understanding and constructive face in situations like that facing Lebanon. As a reasoned peacekeeper in the world and to ensure that Canada's views are part of world opinion, I urge the Government to take whatever steps are necessary to be part of a successful ceasefire undertaking in this battle weary region of the world.

Mr. Speaker, my riding is situated exactly half way between Calgary and Edmonton. We have an awful lot of hockey fans and you can understand that during the regular NEIL season the loyalties of my constituents are split fairly evenly.

Mr. Speaker, the Government's family violence initiatives amount to only $10 per battered woman per year. This is not enough to educate society on the seriousness of wife assault.

Sometimes judges may think they are preserving the family unit by handing down lenient sentences, but the family unit is already destroyed by violence. There are not enough programs for men who batter.
Sometimes judges may think lenient sentences are appropriate because the batterer is the breadwinner, but it is dangerous for women and children to be financially dependent on a batterer. Some 40 per cent of all homicides in this country involve domestic violence. Women need economic equality, not dependence on abusers.
The Government has shown itself incompetent in dealing with the problems of family abuse. How many women must lie unconscious or die before we see government action?

subtopic: IMPACT OF RUMOURED RESIGNATION OF MINISTER
IMPACT OF RUMOURED RESIGNATION OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week there were rumours in the international financial community that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was about to or had resigned.
The response to those rumours was dramatic. There was a big sell-off of Canadian dollars in the international monetary market in the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. The Canadian dollar dropped by almost two-thirds of a cent to its lowest level in five months. The Canadian money supply was devalued by $20 billion in a single day. As a result, the Bank of Canada was forced to increase its interest rate to 12.4 per cent in order to support the dollar.
This is clear evidence of the regard the financial community holds the Minister in. Canada is fortunate to have him as its Finance Minister. When the mere rumour of the man's resignation can impact on this country in the value of $20 billion, Canada cannot afford even the slightest chance that this man will abdicate his responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, NATO is presently undergoing a serious internal dispute about the United States Government's desire to introduce a new generation of tactical nuclear missiles to be stationed in West Germany. Canada's membership in NATO is valued, in part, for the opportunity it affords in the promotion of arms control and disarmament.
The Conservative Government should therefore be more active in this dispute by promoting possible NATO alternatives that could include: first, tying the modernization of these nuclear missiles with talks on substantial reductions in the Soviet Union's short-range nuclear arsenal and/or reductions in Warsaw Pact conventional forces; second, adopting a build-down strategy by phasing out other tactical nuclear weapons and only retaining modernized nuclear missiles; and third, substituting the modernization of these missiles with the introduction of non-nuclear smart technology weapons.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) should present these positions during the upcoming NATO meeting and thereafter inform this House about the outcome of any Canadian initiative.

SEVENTY-FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF INDEPENDENCE OF ARMENIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, May 28 is the seventy-first anniversary of the independence of Armenia as declared in 1918.
Armenia has suffered a history of racially motivated genocide, betrayal, persecution, and terrorism. The dream of the Armenian people, however, has not been crushed and their struggle for recognition and independence continues.

May 26. 1989

May 28 commemorates a nation that has suffered extreme adversity and has risen to the challenge. I would like to laud the Armenian people in Don Valley North and throughout the world on their determination to overcome their many obstacles and setbacks on their declared day of independence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: TIMING OF BRIEFING OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I want to ask the Minister about the Government's conspiracy to bury the truth from Canadians about his handling of the budget leaks, a conspiracy about which it has been found out.

At 1.30 or 1.40 before that Question Period, an official of his Department or his office received a call from the president of Mutual Life who informed that individual that Mutual Life had a copy of the Budget in Brief and there was therefore a second, more serious budget leak.
I want to ask the Minister this: Does he expect Canadians to believe that he was not briefed by his officials in the some 20 minutes between the call from the president of Mutual Life and two o'clock and the period of 15 minutes for Members' Statements between two o'clock and 2.15, and that he was not informed by note during the 45 minutes for questions on that day about this second budget leak? Does he expect Canadians to believe that his officials are so incompetent? Why does he not tell us what really happened?

Mr. Speaker, it is not material, why or what. It is what the decision was and I have made it very clear as to why we did not make that material public. We had set in train a course on Wednesday night. The information in the Budget in Brief was a matter of public record through the Global Television Network. We felt it was essential to get that information out in the public record. At that time the process had started.
We continued with that process during the course of Thursday at 11 o'clock, when I stood in the House and explained to the House at the first opportunity I had to get into the House, why we did those things. That process continued.
The decisions that were taken were consistent with that process. We felt it was in the public interest to get that information into the public domain. Many decisions took place during the course of the day. I believe it would have been irresponsible for us to change that process, cause those decisions to be taken based on information that was subsequently withdrawn. So we continued that process. That was consistent with our decision not to make the information on the Mutual Life leak known publicly, because we had also started an RCMP investigation. We did not want to undermine that investigation by making that information public.
I have made that clear and it is very consistent with long-standing practice that we quoted in the House yesterday, based on statements that have been made by members of the Government that he has supported for many years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also addressed to the Minister of Finance. I have always held the Minister of Finance in high regard. I find that today we are changing the traditional principles on budget secrecy.
I would just like him to respond to the people of Canada with the new standards for budget secrecy.

subtopic: SUGGESTION OF EXISTENCE OF NEW STANDARDS FOR BUDGET SECRECY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that we demonstrated very clearly our commitment to budget secrecy on Wednesday evening, April 26. When we found out that the Budget in Brief document was in the hands of Global Television we went immediately to the RCMP and initiated an investigation.
We also went immediately to the Leader of the Opposition and to the Leader of the New Democratic Party and said: "In the interests of our concerns for budget secrecy, and in the interests of our concern to ensure that that information is made available to all Canadian people at the earliest possible date, can we come back to the House of Commons so that the Minister of Finance can read his budget speech?''
That was our commitment to budget secrecy at that time. We believe that we acted responsibly and quickly in order to carry out our responsibilities.
That request was turned down. The first thing that we did after that was to make available that information to Canadians at large through the media by giving a press conference and making available the full package of budget information that at that time had been made available to Members of the House through the Clerk of the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley) moved:
subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FOREST INDUSTRY REDUCTION OF ACID RAIN CAUSING EMISSIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of creating a more stable and sustainable forestry industry taking all measures to reduce acid-rain causing emissions produced in Canada, and flowing across our borders from other countries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to be able to rise today to speak on this motion which, in terms of direct work in the House, is the first motion of substance that I believe we have had to deal with when it comes to the impact of acid rain on our forests.
I am pleased to see some of my colleagues from the Forestry and Fisheries Committee in the House today. I hope we will have a chance to hear their views on this matter.
I want to read the motion for the record because I believe it is important that we have the context of what our debate is about this afternoon. It states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of creating a more stable and sustainable forest industry taking all measures to reduce acid-rain causing emissions produced in Canada, and flowing across our borders from other countries.
That motion is important because I believe all Members, particularly those from central and eastern Canada, are acutely aware of the importance of this issue. Many of us from western Canada, including my home province of British Columbia, are now becoming aware of the impact of acid rain on our forests.
In my comments this afternoon I would like to refer to a number of documents that I believe make the point about how important it is that this House and the Government deal with acid rain and its impact on our forests.
I want to read into the record a few comments that may help us refresh our memories about acid rain, how it is generated, how it is measured, and what its impact really is, particularly on our forests.
Forestry
Acidic precipitation is the correct term for acid rain. This issue has been in the headlines in this country for the last six to ten years when I think Canadians have become generally more aware of their environment.
When acid rain was first discovered, primarily in a number of lakes around Ontario, it was thought to be a local problem. As perhaps with many environmental problems these days, we first become aware of them and it is not until later that we are aware of the national and global implications. We have seen this happen in Ontario, across eastern and central Canada and indeed in the United States.
The Library of Parliament report states that acidic precipitation is derived principally from emissions of sulphur and nitrogen oxides which are released to the environment during the combustion of fossil fuels in the smelting of sulphide ores.
As the pollutants are transported for hundreds or perhaps thousands of kilometres through the atmosphere, the oxides enter into a complex series of chemical reactions to form acids. Sulphuric and nitric acids are the most frequently found types.
The reference to the distances involved pertains to the coal-powered electrical generating stations in the United States and other areas. The tragedy of acid rain is its ability to be carried for great distances into Canada and throughout North America. That is one of the most difficult problems in terms of attempting to get an agreement between our country and the United States.
The global nature of the problem is an important issue with which we must deal in those discussions.
I also want to give some scientific information in terms of how we measure that acid rain. Again, the Library of Parliament report states that acidity is a measure of the concentration of hydrogen ions in solution. As concentration of hydrogen ions increases the solution, water, becomes more acidic and conversely, as the concentration of hydrogen ions decrease the solution becomes less acidic, or more alkaline. Acids are compounds which release hydrogen ions upon dissociation, thus when they are added to water they make it acidic. I am not a scientist, but obviously the general public who are concerned about our forests are aware of what acid rain means and its impact on our lakes and forests throughout the country. I do not think it takes scientists to understand the impact of acid rain on our country. The

May 26, 1989
Forestry
general public is well aware, and often the first to be aware of these problems.
What does it mean for our forests? I want to refer to a statement from the Canadian Institute of Forestry, a most recent report from the Library of Parliament, and a recent report that was commissioned by the federal Government under the Canadian Forestry Service.
The statement by the Canadian Institute of Forestry sums it up best, as perhaps it would, being directly involved in the industry. They state that in eastern Canada, particularly in the sugar maple industry, the trees are suffering particularly from acid rain. I will make reference to a federal report on that matter in a few moments. The Canadian Institute of Forestry cite the year 1995 as when our forests will be facing some very severe problems as a result of acid rain. However, I believe the mounting evidence suggests that we undoubtedly have a problem now with acid rain in our forests.
Perhaps the most important problem we face in dealing with acid rain is the fact that the ecosystems of our forests are so complex. There are many different organisms, different plants, different kinds of trees, so that solving the problem of acid rain on some trees could cause severe problems elsewhere, undoubtedly many of which we are unaware.
The statement goes on to say that many authorities believe the primary effect of acid rain on forest vegetation is the disruption of tree nutrition. It is recognized that some positive effects have resulted because of acid rain. Since different chemicals react in different ways, there might very well be, in some sense, a positive reaction. However, the major problem with which we are faced is the result of a negative reaction. In fact, they go on to say in their statement that most of the effects are expected to be negative and include damage to the structure of the foliage, and accelerated removal of nutrients or moisture from the trees.
Some of the indirect negative effects include increased soil acidity, interference with the nitrogen cycle, accelerated leeching of nutrients from the soil and the release of toxic elements such as aluminium, which are normally
chemically bound in the soil but when released can reduce nutrient uptake by tree roots.
One of the most tragic side effects of that is that it in fact weakens the trees. A weakened tree means that pests have a greater opportunity to invade and to make homes and continue the destruction of the forest as a result of the acid rain.
The federal Government report which I mentioned, which was produced for the Canadian Forestry Service in March of 1986, actually did some sampling and tests in the eastern Quebec area, and there is a map included with this report. It in fact cited that: "Growth rates of sugar maple, white spruce and red spruce have declined sharply since 1950". They are learning that that is directly the result of acid rain and the many problems that we have there.
I would just like to refer to a more recent report, a Library of Parliament report that was released earlier this year. It states the very important damage that is happening to our forests across the country, and in particular the sugar maples in eastern Canada. The report from the Library states that some 40 million hectares of forests in eastern Canada and another seven million in western Canada are seriously affected by airborne pollution.
That is an incredible statement in terms of the impact that acid rain is having on the forests. In fact, some people have called acid rain the AIDS of the trees. That is not to make light of a very serious situation but it points out the gravity of the problem and how immense it is.
A review of the report, which appeared in the Vancouver Sun cites in fact some indications of problems showing up in western Canada.
The report is quoted as saying that: "Half of the sugar maples are affected and 15 per cent of them are already dead," because of acid rain. It further states that: "If the decline continues at the current rate, only a handful of maple stands will remain in Quebec by the end of the next decade."
I know my colleagues on the Forestry and Fisheries Committee are certainly talking about the importance of forestry, not just the impact of acid rain on the forests, but the importance of forests in general to all Canadians.
I know that in our discussions in the committee we have
May 26, 1989

talked about how it is our job, our responsibility to do what we can to draw the importance of the forests to the attention of this House and in turn to all Canadians. There are a number of people whose occupations and lives depend on the forests in many communities across our country.
I know our forestry committee will undoubtedly be dealing with this further and discussing it as we go along.
The problem is not confined just to central or eastern Canada. We now have some indications of acid rain being suspected in British Columbia. The evidence I have here is a very recent news report in the Vancouver Sun, which reports about some arbutus trees and the problems of acid rain on those trees. I gather there is some question about just whether it is in fact acid rain that is causing the problem. Nevertheless, there is evidence from the previous record and some of the problems that have been talked about certainly in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia, where the provincial minister of the environment has finally recognized the fact that that is a major problem. This problem will continue to grow unless we deal with the problem of acid rain on our forests, and many of the problems in general that are related to forestry in the country.
What has been done or what is being proposed? That is the subject of my motion where I call on the Government, as I say in it, to produce a sustainable forest industry that takes action on reducing acid rain and its impact on our forests.
Members will know that in our country there are a number of joint federal-provincial forestry agreements. There has been a lot of debate in this Chamber and in our forestry committee about those agreements and their importance, as well as the importance of what those agreements can do, to the provinces, to the industry and labour and all of the people involved in the forestry industry. In fact, I make reference to one particular agreement in eastern Canada that the federal Government has in the Province of Quebec where they are going to be spending some funds for accelerated research program-and I am quoting from the Estimates- which will include the examination of fertilization as a means to treat affected areas.
Forestry
I think that directly ties in with the debate that has been in this House and in the committee as of late about the importance of the forestry agreements.
In the few minutes that are remaining to me I would like to tie in the major concerns about acid rain and its impact on our forests with some of the vehicles and chosen methods that we can use to try and solve with that problem. That is a forestry agreement that has been proposed between the federal and provincial governments, in this case Quebec.
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House, that these agreements have proven to be effective vehicles for the different levels of Government to achieve various aims, and in this case in our forest industry. Those FRDAs, as they are called, and this is a particular FRDA, a Forest Resource Development Agreement, is a vehicle to achieve sustainable development and some planning in our forests.
In the case of Ontario, we have a forest agreement that is in limbo right now. The Minister in the committee the other day suggested to us that he would not release his criteria that he wants to use to negotiate a new agreement with Ontario and the other provinces. I would suggest that in Ontario there is a role for this committee and for the House to know exactly what criteria this level of government can use in co-operation with the province to try and resolve the problems that we have with acid rain in the Province of Ontario and other provinces.
As you probably know, Mr. Speaker, the Minister has talked a lot about long-term planning in forestry. We have been pursuing that with the Minister in committee, in terms of what he mean by that. Does he have the 20-year plans in place from the provinces that the initial FRDA agreements called for.
We are looking forward to that, and we hope that the Minister deals with the six provinces that are due. We know that he has called an early meeting of the forestry ministers across the country for June. I suggest that June is time for some action so that we can deal with this. The reason I mentioned the forestry agreements is because that is one of the most important ways that this Government and our provincial governments can attempt to implement some of the policies and the research that is needed to solve and deal with acid rain's impact on our forests.

May 26, 1989
Forestry
On a broader scope, in coming to a conclusion, it is regrettable and unfortunate to have to finish on a negative note on this because we have heard time and time again from this Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about his special relationship with the President of the United States and how he is going to be able to resolve and deal with acid rain.
We have not seen that, despite this special relationship. I asked one of my colleagues, the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) who is our noted environment critic: "What happened to Bill Davis?" What did happen to Bill Davis? What was his contribution in trying to solve the impact of acid rain on Canada and in our forests? I think that the Government itself would admit that Mr. Davis and whatever he was doing-and I was not a Member of the House at that time-was an absolute failure.
There is much that remains to be done. The importance of signing an agreement between Canada and the United States will help resolve the general over-all problem of acid rain and its impact on our environment, and in particular, its impact on our forests where so many people have their livelihoods, and so many communities depend on it, and so many people are now beginning to understand the importance of that industry to our ecosystems and to our way of life in this country.

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FOREST INDUSTRY REDUCTION OF ACID RAIN CAUSING EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this motion which the Hon. Member from Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. Gardiner) has put before the House.
I want to emphasize that this motion states the obvious, but it comes quite a long time after policy directions were taken by the Government. The substance of the motion deals with having a more stable and sustainable forest industry and reducing acid rain causing emissions.
The Throne Speech at the beginning of this session stated some things very clearly. One, of course, was the environmental imperative in which the subject of acid rain was a very significant component. During the debates that followed it, we voiced on more than one occasion the objective of an acid rain accord with the United States.
In this session, during the budget debate and elsewhere, we have heard references to the new fullyfledged Department of Forestry which is being created by the Government and which will, I hope and trust, give significant new emphasis to the forests and all of the resources associated with them in the months and the years to come.
I have the privilege of being a member of two standing committees of this House, the Forestry and Fisheries Committee and the Environment Committee. Initiatives are now under way in both areas.
I believe that among other subjects we will be addressing in the forestry committee are terms of reference for the new Department of Forestry. In so doing, we will be addressing a stable and sustained forest economy, forest industry, forest ecology and forest environment in this country. We will give the significance to the forests of Canada that they deserve. We will help the Minister hopefully, and the other departments of Government to reconcile and resolve those many areas that overlap, and sometimes cause conflict. Multiple use forest management requires intensive co-operation and perhaps, in fact, requires some transfers of mandate from one department to another.
In terms of the environment, already in our environmental committee we have talked about the concepts of sustainable development as enunciated so well in the World Commission on the Environment and Development, the so-called Brundtland Report. I have already recommended to that committee that we use forestry as one of the subject areas to develop concepts of sustainable development in Canada's future. I think that forestry is a very apt subject in that respect.
I recognize that the Hon. Member from Prince George comes from an area where forestry is of great value in terms of employment, economics, ecology, recreation and aesthetics. I understand that because I come from New Brunswick where the forest is also extremely important. More than one-third of our entire provincial economy in New Brunswick is related to forestry. We all realize Canada's forests go far beyond their economic value. The Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Oberle) has described on more than one occasion that he sees Canada's forests as an analogy to the human body. He describes them as the very lungs and kidneys of an ecosystem. Forests help to regulate the atmosphere by trapping and converting solar energy into oxygen. They also play an important role in controlling global precipitation and moisture exchange. It is therefore imperative that we direct our efforts to ensuring that Canada's
May 26, 1989

forests, as part of the global life support system, remain healthy and flourishing.
We must strive to do better than we have. That is not to say we have not done well, that we have not significantly started to manage our forests in a more comprehensive and intense way than was the case prior to the recognition of concepts such as sustainable development and the impact of the environment and the developing knowledge on subjects such as acid rain. We have much more to do. Sustainable development and other concepts will lead us to new horizons and new challenges.
I would like to say again, and I apologize for being parochial, that New Brunswick has shown the way in terms of forest management legislation in Canada. I believe that those who would address improved forest management in this country should address themselves to the Crown Lands and Forests Act in New Brunswick. They should also address themselves to the steps which have been taken over the past five years by officials, scientists and managers of the forests in New Brunswick as they have implemented the terms and conditions of the new legislation for multiple use and more intensive management addressing both Crown and private lands.

Mr. Speaker, the management of forests in Canada is a major concern of our Government. Forestry Canada managers will describe for Hon. Members the work done by the federal Government concerning the health of forests as it regards the forestry industry. We are all aware that the management problems include climate, insects, diseases, management practices and air pollution. In addition, as the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. Gardiner) said, the facts point increasingly to acid rain as a killer of forests.
I would nevertheless like to emphasize that this Government recognizes that it can no longer wait to have all the scientific data in hand before proceeding. Once the trees are gone, it will no longer do much good to understand in depth the cause of this disaster-it will be too late.
Forestry

As proof of how seriously the Conservative Government takes finding a long-term solution to the problems of acid rain, I would like to review for the House the acid rain control program that has been put in place in this country to end the environmental, economic and health-related damages being caused by acid rain.
The Hon. Member has already described many of the causes, results and severe impacts of acid rain. I will not repeat those, but I will talk a bit about what the Government has done.
I am proud to remind this House that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced in March, 1985 that Canada would implement a comprehensive ten year acid rain control program estimated to cost $500 million annually when fully implemented in 1994. The federal Government, in partnership with the seven eastern provincial Governments and affected industries, has established a clear, scientifically derived objective for resolving Canada's acid rain problem. Canadian scientists have established that to prevent acid rain damage, acid rain fallout must be reduced to less than 20 kilograms per hectare per year in all vulnerable areas. To achieve this environmental objective requires two things.
First, total Canadian emissions of sulphur dioxide from the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border eastward must be reduced to 2.3 million tonnes per year. This represents a 50 per cent cut in emissions from 1980 allowable levels.
I see I am running out of time, Mr. Speaker, so I will proceed more quickly and say that Canada's acid rain control program is achieving the required results. Emissions levels are now below 2.8 million tonnes per year in eastern Canada, almost 40 per cent below the levels allowed in 1980. It is clear that we will reach our goal of a 50 per cent reduction in domestic emissions by 1994 or earlier.
I would also like to say that we do require a formal accord on acid rain between the United States and Canada. In the recent visit by President Bush, there are clear signals that an accord is achievable and that negotiations and relations are well under way between our two countries for its achievement.

May 26, 1989
Forestry
I would say that this motion, while so well intentioned and comprehensive, is well behind the leading edge of government policy and action on these two important fronts, both in forestry and environment. On acid rain, Canada is and has been on the move.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on this important issue.
Acid rain is a bilateral problem that must be addressed through bilateral channels. I will be talking about that. I also want to emphasize the phenomenon of the long-range transport of atmospheric pollutants and the potential accumulative affect it has on the environmental problems in my riding.
The environmental problems facing the North are extensive. The most serious include Arctic toxic pollution, ozone destruction, and the greenhouse effect. Canadians have made it clear that they want this country to take action on its many environmental problems, problems which are shared internationally. A new environmental responsibility is a political imperative, but it is also an undeniable necessity.
Our planet is diseased by man's environmental neglect. Human beings, indeed all living beings, are suffering the side effects. In Canada's North, we find that some Inuit people are ingesting unacceptable levels of PCBs.
Most environmental damage is irreversible and the accumulative effects are degrading the environment at an astounding rate. In the last 100 years, man has done infinitely more damage to the planet than since humans appeared on the scene millions of years ago.
Today, we are at an historical transition between a world inherited and one profoundly different, a global biosphere whose vital functions we have altered.
Do we want future generations to inherit an exhausted planet with which they will live at odds, or do we want to leave a heritage of health and harmony, a society with a clean house and values to keep it that way? Obviously, we want the latter.
Humans can adapt this value to live in harmony with the environment. It will require re-examination of materialism and modern development, but there is no reason to believe the challenge cannot be met.
By treating our environment right, we will be treating ourselves right. This is what will breed kinder and gentler nations.
Canada must lead the world in practising environmentally responsible statecraft. This means defining and implementing a strict concept of sustainable development, securing global co-operation to immediately eliminate critical problems, and fostering an environmentally-conscious populace through public education and involvement.
Ranging across some 30 per cent of the planet's land surface, forests have been described as "the climax ecosystems of a green and flowering world-the most exuberant expressions of nature." Forests perform protective, productive and regulative functions. They play a vital ecological role in the planetary recycling of oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon. They influence temperature and rainfall. They act as enormous sponges, collecting and distributing water. They protect the soil from water and wind erosion. They maintain biological diversity. They actively contribute to economic development.
Recently, however, new problems such as acid rain and other air pollutants have emerged which may stress forests beyond their regenerative capacities.
Forest management is the keystone of a natural resource conservation strategy.
Canada is a world leader in forestry. No country trades more extensively in global forest products, the latter accounting for 15 to 20 per cent of Canada's total export earnings. Over the years, Canadians have developed a broad range of modern forestry skills and techniques, and much of this technology has proved to be adaptable to tropical forest conditions.
Acid rain potentially may affect all sectors of the environment, including human health. The most persuasive evidence has been assembled for aquatic systems. It is now well known that freshwater bodies begin to show biological damage at about a very moderate level of acidity. It is feared that forests, in particular, are being damaged by acid rain and by associated pollutants such as ozone. It is also known that man-made materials are susceptible to damage from acid rain and from associated air pollutants.
May 26, 1989

Not only is the dollar cost of acid-rain damage to buildings and other structures very high, but treasured artifacts, including sculpture and historic sites, are threatened with destruction.
When I gave my speech in response to the Budget on May 18,1 stated that Canada needs to develop a foreign policy and not just a defence policy for cruise missile tests and nuclear submarines, but that a foreign policy should be all encompassing with global environmental security as a cornerstone. We need to push for acceleration of the ozone protocol, adoption of an international law of the air, measures to ensure rapid reduction in the C02 level, and preservation of tropical rain forests.
Taken together, these measures represent a comprehensive and coherent approach to our environment covering preventive, punitive, and remedial action as well as domestic and international aspects. They demonstrate the proactive liberal approach to this crucial issue and are based on the fundamental premise that pollution is everyone's problem; that we must all work together to ensure a healthy and secure environment for future generations. Sustainable development for the forest industry needs to be defined and must be complemented by comprehensive and extensive national environmental objectives.
My constituents of Western Arctic are concerned that Alberta's massive forestry development has potential to threaten one of Canada's largest and cleanest river systems and massive tracts of northern forests. Seven pulp mills are planned for the Peace-Athabasca River system, the source of most water in the southwestern N.W.T. and northern Alberta. The concept of sustainable development must be applied to this proposal. The economic benefits need to be recognized, but the negative impacts of the project must be minimized. The Government must be held accountable to implement a strict sustainable development regime in good faith.
On May 11, the Member from Davenport asked the Government House Leader when he would introduce a motion to strike the standing committee on acid rain which was in existence until the call of the election. We have heard nothing from the Government.
As usual, this Government will not move fast enough. Regulations are a necessary part of environmental man-
Forestry
agement. As trustees of the environment, governments must act with vigour to protect it. Governments must lead with comprehensive support and promotion of sustainable economic development.
This Government has to change the way it approaches the environment and the economy. It has to integrate environmental input into decision-making at the highest level. Environment must be a priority of every federal Department.
My Party recommends an auditor general for the environment. Environmental considerations cannot be an add-on or an afterthought. They must be made integral to economic policy-making and planning and a required element of any economic development proposal.
I want to re-emphasize, in conclusion, that acid rain is a problem that wafts across borders. Acid rain, snow, and fog kill fish and other aquatic biota and damage forests in Canada, the U.S., and western and central Europe. An estimated 200,000 square miles of forests in industrial countries are damaged by acid rain or other forms of air pollution. It demands international solutions. As well, discussion of long-range transport of air pollutants can no longer be restricted to oxides of sulphur and nitrogen. Hydrocarbons are interacting with these gases at low atmospheric levels, producing damaging ozone. Toxic pollutants such as pesticides, metals and PCBs are being emitted and volatilizing from aerial sprayings and open bodies of water to be deposited at great distances away. The ecological damage of acid rain is generally understood, but the associated human morbidity and potential long-term health effects are not.
Pollutants in the environment can wreak unforeseen results, among them a global warming trend that could push average temperatures higher than any in the experience of the human race. A nuclear winter caused by global war might mean the end of most life forms. Yet along with potential self-destruction, the present moment of technology's course has delivered tools of knowledge never before in hand. What is the Government waiting for? We have the tools to do something.

May 26, 1989
Forestry
