speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate ray colleague on an excellent presentation concerning the problem of acid rain and its damage to forests. Coming from a region where a great number of my constituents earn their living from the forests, naturally I am interested in this whole question.
In 1982, with the help of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, I organized and sponsored a seminar on the problem that faced our forests, that being acid rain. We had gathered enough evidence to show that, as most Canadians know, the pulp and paper industry in this country is of extreme importance. Its importance cannot be exaggerated. Study after study has pointed to the fact that acid rain is something that is visible, it is concrete and obviously we have got to tackle the problem.
I am sure that in this House the concern about acid rain goes above Party lines. There is no doubt about that in my mind. Our own sulphur emissions need to be under control, and I am sure that we will tackle that problem with great vigour. However, we have a problem with our neighbours to the south. Study after study does not seem to convince them that we need an absolute commitment to seriously limit the problem of sulphur emissions that create acid rain. The Canadian Pulp and Paper Association has conducted extended studies. These have indicated that if the trend continues within the next quarter century, there will be no more pulp and paper industry in this country. This is incredible when we consider that this country had such tremendous forest reserves. We are surrounded literally by forests. Within 30 minutes of my home town, I can literally be lost in the wilderness. Nevertheless this danger is mounting week by week to the point where our whole forest industry is in severe danger.
Needless to say, we do not want to be portrayed as alarmists, but the fact remains that acid rain is probably the greatest threat facing the forest industry. Yet, it does not stop with our forest industry. There was a series of interesting programs on the CBC about a year and a half to two years ago that pointed out the danger to our forest industry. They also showed that if this damage continues, there will be social unrest in our country because the industry will be on the verge of being eliminated. We cannot exaggerate the importance.
Surely all Members of this House would want our Government to be insistent-and we will not accept no or maybe for an answer-and indicate to our industries, which we are doing, and indicate to our neighbour to the south that its northeastern states are affected. We in particular are being affected. I have met with the maple syrup producers in my area and they are seeing the damage year by year.
Like all Members of this House, we will appeal as forcefully as we can to our friendly neighbours to the south for an agreement. We are willing to put a tremendous amount of water in our wine if we have to, but we need a commitment and a reduction or else we will live to see the damage to our forest industry if it is not corrected. That is the issue that faces one of our major industries. It would probably be the greatest catastrophe of our lifetime.
It is imperative that we stand up and be counted and let them know, not only to the south, but everywhere, that Canada is going to solve its acid rain problem even if we have to take radical steps. We will call upon our neighbours to the south in the northeastern states to join us to make our two Governments understand that the time has come to correct the problem. We do not want to live with a catastrophe on our hands. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for this time that has been allotted to me.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on a motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. Gardiner), a fellow member on the Forestry and Fisheries Committee. The Hon. Member represents a riding, like mine, where the forestry industry has created many jobs for a number of years, jobs that have benefited several generations. Our constituents also realize that forestry operations are extremely important to the economy of our ridings and to the economy of this coutry.
Mr. Speaker, our forests are one of our major resources. They cover nearly half of Canada's total area and, south of the sixtieth parallel, cover almost two-thirds of our territory. Logging has stimulated economic growth in Canada since the time of the huge annual log drives on Canada's rivers. Today, the forestry industry consist of about 7,000 companies, most of which are
May 26, 1989

Canadian-owned. These companies are responsible for about 4 per cent of Canada's Gross Domestic Product. Annual sales in the industry amount to $30 billion, and in 1987, our exports of forestry products were worth over $21 billion. We have here an industry that is extremely important to Canada, an industry that creates many jobs and contributes to the economic stability and prosperity of many regions in this country.
The problem we are discussing today, the deterioration of our forests, is a major one, and at this point I would like to mention that the present Government has met the problem head-on and taken steps and introduced mechanisms to respond to this challenge. The challenge we are facing is that of maintaining healthy forests so that the industry and this natural resource will continue to contribute to the well-being of Canadians.
I believe that our Government has recognized the importance of the forestry industry by appointing to the Cabinet a full Minister responsible for forestry and forestry policy in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should also remember that the Prime Minister comes from a region that grew up and developed thanks to the forestry industry which still exists in Baie-Comeau and on the North Shore, and also in my own riding where forestry operations have existed since the turn of the century.
The problem we are discussing today is an important one, but acid rain is not the only problem affecting the viability and health of our forests. There are many other causes such as insects, logging, of course, and natural causes that annually contribute to the destruction of hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest in Canada. Forest fires also do considerable damage. We are looking at a complex problem, and as a responsible Government, we must take a comprehensive approach if we are to implement a sound and consistent policy that will both ensure that our forestry industry remains economically viable and help maintain the quality of our environment, clean up air pollution and thus make it possible for all Canadians to continue to rely on this major natural resource and also enjoy the recreational opportunities it offers.
Forestry
I can assure the Elon. Member that his contribution and mine to the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries should help provide for a fair policy, as proposed by our Government, a policy that will be maintained during the next four years, a policy that is consistent, intelligent and a sensible; a policy that will help provide jobs and ensure that our environment is both protected and profitable.

subsubtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FOREST INDUSTRY REDUCTION OF ACID RAIN CAUSING EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. Gardiner), has raised a very important issue. I welcome the opportunity to speak on that issue. It is important to all Canadians.
The Hon. Member has chosen to direct his motion toward a single factor affecting that particular issue and that is acid rain. No one will question the fact that the Government is concerned about the problems of pollution, acid rain, and transborder emissions that affect all of us. No one would argue that the United States is equally concerned. In the Speech from the Throne earlier this session we stated that we are going to address that problem and seek agreement with the United States to bring this international problem under control.
Since 1984 the Government has continued to push forward in this area, as all Canadians are demanding, for a solution to those problems and ensuring that they are dealt with head-on. The 1987 Ozone Protocol signed in Montreal is another indication that the Government is serious about the problem, is doing something about it, and will continue to work on an international scale.
The protection of the environment will be one of the main goals of the Government in its second mandate. If we are going to have sustained economic development in this country that will go beyond our life expectancy into that of our children, we must address those very real problems. It is a concern that is being expressed by all Canadians. It was certainly expressed throughout the campaign last fall. Canadians of all ages, young and old alike-and many who were well below the voting age attending high school or university-spoke out and indicated very clearly that they wanted whatever

May 26, 1989
Forestry
Government was elected to put this issue on its agenda. We have chosen to deal with that.
The link between air pollution and the decline of our forests is easy to make for anyone who has visited such places as Trail, British Columbia or Sudbury, Ontario. One only need look out of a car window or the window of an airplane to see the effects. It is a very complex problem. I am not sure one single factor is the reason. Is acid rain the only reason our forests are dying? I contend that it is not the sole reason and that there are other factors.
If one looks at some of the highly industrialized areas of the country and the effect that they have on the surrounding environment and the volatile organic compounds, other oxidants, and heavy metals that are present in the ground, they are also having an effect. We have to consider many factors when looking at our dying forests and the problem areas throughout the country. Acid rain is a key topic and it is one that we can clearly point our finger at, but it is not the only one.
The distinction between acid rain problems and other environmental problems is very difficult to make. Some highly regarded experts are having difficulty making the distinction, is it acid rain or is it something else? It is a very broad topic. The Government is concerned about it, and we are going to work hard in that regard. We have committed ourselves to it, and we are going to follow through with it.
Canada is not alone in this regard. The U.S. is very concerned, as are the European countries. It was back in the heady days of the 1960s and the early 1970s when acid rain became a hot topic. Early in the 1970s the European countries realized the problem and they raised it at an international level. Not long after we in Canada were faced with the same problem.
In my riding of Carleton-Charlotte the forestry sector is indeed a very important sector of our economy. We have the same problem. We are living in an ecological zone that seems to be more susceptible to that problem than other parts of the country. We will continue to monitor the problem closely. We will continue to work as best we can within fiscal restraints to address this problem.
Ultimately the problem will cost Canada jobs. For example, in eastern Canada there are approximately
10,000 maple syrup producers and many small wood lot owners who are affected by this problem. If one goes into the forests of Quebec and looks at this problem, it will be seen that it is very complex. None of us want to see our national symbol, the maple leaf, turn brown. However, in areas such as eastern Quebec and in my province of New Brunswick, the problems go far beyond acid rain. There are some complex questions that scientists are scratching their heads over and to which they have no answers. Of over 100 studies done only two actually point directly to the acid rain problem. There are many other variables which cannot be accounted for. It is a serious problem, and one we are dealing with. We must consider all pollutants, not only the hydrogen sulphites and other gases that directly contribute to acid rain.
In many forests there is an insect problem, or diseases over which the scientists are scratching their heads as to how they came about and exactly what they are, how long-term they will be, and whether we can eradicate them at all. We also have management problems. That problem the Government is addressing in a serious manner. Part of the management of our forests is coming from examples set in my own province of New Brunswick.
The Hon. Member for Fredericton (Mr. Bird) was a former Minister of Forestries in our home province. He is the individual responsible for bringing in that progressive legislation. As a nation we are going to follow the example of the province of New Brunswick, because it has been successful. It has proven that a small province with limited fiscal resources has the ability to deal with the problem.
In conclusion, the problem we have is a complex one. The motion of the Hon. Member opposite is a very narrow motion. We have to go beyond the sense of narrowness that I see in his motion. We as a Government are prepared to go beyond the narrow bounds of that particular motion and recognize that it is a problem that deserves a high degree of energy and a high degree of resource on the part of all of us. I am proud to say that the Minister of State (Forestry) (Mr. Oberle) is working on the problem, that he recognizes it and in time it will be dealt with in the fashion that Canadians wish it to be dealt with.
May 26, 1989
